solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Every so often, setting a mean mark!

indicators.note: taking letters every so often means picking every other letter from the words that follow

explanation.surface: An exclamation about a stingy marker giving out low grades.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Every so often' takes the odd-placed letters of SETTING A MEAN: S, T, I, G, M, A.
explanation.definitionFit: A stigma is a mark of disgrace, and in botany or religion a literal mark or spot, so mark is a synonym.

clue.text: Note doctor brings comfort

parts.note: so (or soh) is the fifth note of the tonic sol-fa scale
to doctor a drink is to lace it, adding something secretly

explanation.surface: A sick note from the doctor brings the patient some relief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doctor' looks like a noun (Dr or MO) but is the verb: to doctor a drink is to lace it.
explanation.definitionFit: Solace is consolation offered in distress, a close synonym of comfort as a noun.

clue.text: Are they organised by CID in Montrose?

definitions.text: Are they organised by CID in Montrose?

indicators.note: the letters of the phrase are organised, set out in a new order

parts.note: CID is the Criminal Investigation Department of a British police force; Montrose is a Scottish town

explanation.surface: A question about how detectives in a Scottish town run their investigations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organised' rearranges CID IN MONTROSE, and the whole clue also describes the answer: such rooms are set up by detectives. Montrose is a small town in Angus, Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: When police open a major case they set up dedicated operations rooms, which detectives from the CID organise and staff.

clue.text: More experienced, but could make erratum

indicators.note: the letters of the word could be made into another word by rearranging them

explanation.surface: Someone more experienced might still slip and make a printing error.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could make' rearranges ERRATUM.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone more mature has had more time to grow and gain experience, a comparative synonym.

clue.text: Requirement to keep dry, now you've landed

indicators.note: one word keeps the other, holding it inside

parts.note: a need is a requirement
TT means teetotal, so dry in the sense of not drinking alcohol

explanation.surface: An angler is told the essential thing is to stay dry, now the catch is ashore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to keep' signals the containment; 'dry' means not drinking alcohol here, not free of water, and the definition reads as a fish just brought ashore.
explanation.definitionFit: To land a fish is to bring it in, and catching it in a net is one way to do so, hence a synonym.

clue.text: Experience for the French going on transport

parts.note: en is the French word for travelling by a means of transport, as in en train or en voiture
a transport of delight is joy or rapture

explanation.surface: Travelling in France, one experiences the local transport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'transport' is not a vehicle but rapture, as in 'transports of delight'.
explanation.definitionFit: To enjoy something such as good health is to have or experience it, a synonym in that sense.

clue.text: What prisoners do when pub closes, repeatedly

parts.note: prisoners do time, serving their sentence
a British pub closes after the landlord calls 'Time!', so closing comes after time

explanation.surface: A joke about what convicts get up to once the pub has shut.
explanation.walkthrough: In British pubs the landlord calls 'Time!' at closing, so the moment the pub closes is after time.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for doing something again and again over many occasions is a common phrase for repeatedly.

clue.text: Stop Des first!

parts.note: the setter's own name, taken as written
first abbreviates to 1st, read with the digit 1 as the letter I

explanation.surface: A plea to put a stop to the setter Des before anyone else.
explanation.walkthrough: Des is this puzzle's setter. The 1 of 1st is read as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: To desist is to cease or refrain from an action, so it matches the verb stop.

clue.text: Cool art forms part of index

indicators.note: the letters given form something new when rearranged

explanation.surface: An index of art books lists cool art as one heading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'forms' rearranges COOL ART.
explanation.definitionFit: In indexing, the page numbers or references that point the reader to each heading are called locators.

clue.text: Farmers organised statue of God outside church

indicators.note: two pieces sit outside a third, enclosing it

parts.note: to run something is to organise it, past tense ran
Eros, the Greek god of love, is famously a statue at Piccadilly Circus in London

explanation.surface: Farmers arranged for a religious statue to be put up around a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside' puts RAN and EROS on either side of CH. 'organised' looks like an anagram signal but means RAN here.
explanation.definitionFit: Rancheros are ranchers, people who farm livestock on ranches in Spanish-speaking America.

clue.text: Old king held back by lese-majesty

indicators.note: the held letters are read back, right to left
the word is held inside the letters of the following text

explanation.surface: A former monarch withheld something because of an offence against the crown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'held' finds SEMAJ inside lESE-MAJesty and 'back' turns it round. Lese-majesty is the crime of insulting a sovereign.
explanation.definitionFit: Several kings of England and Scotland bore this name, such as the Stuart king who succeeded Elizabeth I.

clue.text: Journalist trapped in vehicle that has cones all round it?

definitions.text: that has cones all round it?

indicators.note: one piece is trapped inside the other

parts.note: a car is a vehicle
ED, short for editor, is the usual crossword journalist

explanation.surface: A reporter stuck in a car surrounded by traffic cones at roadworks.
explanation.walkthrough: The cones are fir cones on the tree, not traffic cones; the question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: A conifer bears its seed in cones, which hang all over its branches, so the tree has them all round it.

clue.text: Denies a Yankee, eg, has been entertained by Poles

indicators.note: the inner pieces are entertained, taken in, by the outer one

parts.note: N and S are the north and south poles
Yankee is Y in the NATO phonetic alphabet
say is used like eg, meaning for example

explanation.surface: An American visitor is refused while staying with a Polish family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has been entertained by' puts A, Y and SAY between N and S. 'Poles' are the compass poles, not people from Poland.
explanation.definitionFit: To naysay is to refuse or contradict, so the third-person form matches denies.

clue.text: Stormont House's leader altered extreme position

indicators.note: the letters are altered into a new order

parts.note: Stormont is the seat of the Northern Ireland Assembly in Belfast

indicators.note: a word's leader is its first letter

explanation.surface: The head of Northern Ireland's parliament building changed to a hardline stance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leader' takes H from House's, and 'altered' rearranges STORMONT plus H. Stormont, in Belfast, houses Northern Ireland's Assembly, fitting the northern answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The point furthest towards the north is an extreme, the farthest position in that direction.

clue.text: Golden light round Florida resort

parts.note: or is gold in heraldry
to alight or light is to come down, settle or land
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: A golden glow surrounds a sunny Florida holiday spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'light' is the verb, as a bird lights on a branch: it lands.
explanation.definitionFit: Orlando, home of Disney World and other theme parks, is a well-known holiday city in Florida.

clue.text: Go for a boat trip, touring south

indicators.note: one piece tours round the other, going all about it

parts.note: a sail is a trip in a boat
S is the compass abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: An invitation to take a cruise heading south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'touring' puts S inside A SAIL. 'Go for' reads as 'choose' but means attack.
explanation.definitionFit: To go for someone is to attack them, and assail is a synonym for attacking verbally or physically.

clue.text: French schools, or else youth clubs — initially — reformed

indicators.note: the letters are reformed in another order
initially takes the first letter of each word

explanation.surface: Reorganised schools in France, or else reformed youth clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' takes Y and C from youth clubs; 'reformed' rearranges them with ELSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A lycée is a French state secondary school, preparing pupils for the baccalauréat.

clue.text: Fighter in Canadian feature knocking out Lawrence

indicators.note: a word is knocked out of the longer phrase, removed from it

parts.note: the St Lawrence River is a major Canadian waterway

explanation.surface: A boxer in some Canadian landmark knocks out a man called Lawrence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocking out' removes LAWRENCE from ST LAWRENCE RIVER, leaving ST RIVER. 'Fighter' suggests a boxer but means anyone who strives.
explanation.definitionFit: A striver is someone who struggles or battles hard to achieve something, a fighter in that sense.

clue.text: Roman road circling two lakes and country house

indicators.note: one piece circles round the other, enclosing it

parts.note: via is Latin for road, as in the Via Appia
L is the abbreviation for lake, so two of them is LL

explanation.surface: A Roman road loops past two lakes to a grand country house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'circling' signals the containment; 'Roman' is not decoration but tells you to use the Latin word for road.
explanation.definitionFit: A Roman villa was a country estate house, and the word still means a large house in the country.

clue.text: Regretting replacing first of scooters with large truck

indicators.note: one letter is replaced by another in the word

parts.note: sorry means regretting or apologetic

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: Someone sorry they swapped their scooters for a big truck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'replacing' swaps the S of SORRY (first of 'scooters') for L.
explanation.definitionFit: A lorry is the British word for a large goods vehicle, what Americans call a truck.

clue.text: A ring or chain in water

parts.note: a bell's toll is its ring

explanation.surface: A ring or chain dropped in water, perhaps lost overboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ring' points to the shape of the answer but supplies TOLL, as a bell tolls.
explanation.definitionFit: An atoll is a ring-shaped coral reef or chain of islets surrounding a lagoon in the sea.

clue.text: Dawn insures convertible

indicators.note: convertible letters can be converted into another order

explanation.surface: A woman named Dawn takes out insurance on a convertible car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dawn' looks like a name and 'convertible' like a car; 'convertible' rearranges INSURES.
explanation.definitionFit: Daybreak, when the sun appears over the horizon, is the start of the day: a synonym of dawn.

clue.text: In Dallas, Carol dated sailor

indicators.note: the word lies in the letters of the following text

explanation.surface: A woman called Carol went out with a sailor in Dallas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' finds the word across dalLAS CARol. 'dated' looks like going out together but says the word is old-fashioned.
explanation.definitionFit: A lascar was an East Indian seaman serving on European ships, a term now historical.

clue.text: Cosmetics on faces of the old, not exactly right, somehow

indicators.note: the face of each word is its front, its first letter

explanation.surface: Make-up applied to older faces never looks quite right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on faces of' takes the first letter of each of the six following words. The final word looks like an anagram signal but only supplies its S.
explanation.definitionFit: Toners are skin-care lotions applied to the face after cleansing, a kind of cosmetic product.
